Also, noise points the other way. If a small gain is hard to measure, that's a reason to be *more* careful about calling the team a winner. It's not a reason to lower the bar until it wins. The fix for noise is more questions or more tries, decided before the next run.

"It moves the goalposts after the result" is better because it names the real mistake: changing the rule once you know the outcome, which lets a lucky or disappointing result decide what "winning" means.

check:1:2.q: Why not “The rule should only be about cost”?
check:1:2.a:
**Why "The rule should only be about cost" isn't the best answer**

It does get one thing right. Cost matters. That's why the rule already has a cost limit of 50 cents per success.

But it misses two things.

First, it doesn't answer the question. The problem here is *when* the rule changes, not *what* it measures. Dropping the quality part now, after the team fell short, is just another way of rewriting the rule to fit the result. That's the same mistake as lowering the gain.

Second, a rule about cost alone can't tell you whether the team is *better*. A team could be cheap and still fail more questions than one agent. The quality part, "pass every time on at least 1 more question in 10," is what checks that the team actually does the job better.

**Why "It moves the goalposts after the result" is right**

Moving the goalposts means changing what counts as winning after you've seen the score. The rule was written before any run so it stays fixed. Changing it now lets a disappointing result look like a win.

judge.notes: Minor: the closing explanation runs to three sentences where one was asked for, and 'gain' is used without being explained.

check:2:0.q: Why not “How many tries each question needs”?
check:2:0.a:
That option touches something real. Tries do matter in this experiment. Agents give different answers on different tries, so you run each question 3 to 5 times.

But you choose that number before the experiment starts. It's part of the setup, and it's the same for every design. Adding a third design doesn't tell you anything new about it.

The third design is an **ablation**. That means taking one part out to see what changes. Here, the part removed is the checker. The two teams are the same in every other way: same questions, same number of tries, same scoring. So comparing them points straight at the checker.

In the lesson's example, the team passed every time on 15 of 20 questions, and the team without its checker on 12 of 20. That 3-question gap is your best evidence for the checker's value. Some of it could still be luck, since tries vary. That's why you repeat tries and write the decision rule first.

"What the checker adds to the team" is better because removing only the checker makes the gap between the two teams a measure of that one part.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Whether the team beats one agent”?
check:2:1.a:
"Whether the team beats one agent" is a real question in this experiment. It just isn't the one the third design answers.

**What it gets right:** the experiment does test whether the team beats one agent. That answer comes from comparing the full team against the **baseline** (the one agent, the design you compare against). In the example, the team passed every time on 15 of 20 questions and the one agent on 12. You don't need the third design for that.

**What it misses:** the third design is the team with one part removed, its checker. That is an **ablation**: you take one piece out and see what changes. Its job is to show what that one piece does. So you compare it with the full team, not with the one agent. In the example, the full team passed every time on 15 of 20 and the team without its checker on 12. That gap is the checker's work. It also shows the team without a checker did no better than one agent.

"What the checker adds to the team" is better because it names exactly what the third design measures: the difference made by removing one part.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Run each design several times” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
Agents don't give the same answer every time. The model picks its words with some randomness. So the same question can pass on one try and fail on the next.

That makes a single run like a single coin flip. If the team passes 2 more questions than the one agent on one run, the gap might be real. Or it might be luck.

**What goes wrong in real work:** say you run each design once on 20 questions. The team passes 14 and the one agent passes 12. You ship the team, even though each success costs about nine times more. A week later, users hit the same failures as before. The team was never better. It just had a good run.

Running each question 3 to 5 times fixes this. A question counts as "passed every time" only if all its tries passed. A lucky pass no longer counts, because one failed try cancels it.

Now the comparison asks "which design is reliably right?" instead of "which design got lucky once?" With a decision rule written before any run, that makes the test fair.

judge.notes: No real problem. The 'nine times more' cost remark is a little distracting, since the lesson's rule would accept $0.35 per success, but it does not contradict the lesson.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Score both designs, then apply the rule” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second answer**

*The problem.* Agents give different answers on different tries. So one lucky run can make a team of agents look better than it really is.

*The idea.* I run both designs on the same questions, 3 to 5 times each. One agent is the baseline, the design I compare against. A question counts only if every try passed. That gives each design a score. Then I apply a decision rule I wrote before any run. For example: the team must pass every time on at least 1 more question in 10, at 50 cents or less per success. Writing the rule first means I can't move the goalposts after I see results.

*The trade-off.* Repeated tries cost time and money. Also, a team might win because of one part. So I test a third design: the team without its checker. That's an ablation, which means removing one part to see what changes.

**A likely follow-up**

"Why not just average the pass rate across tries?"

Hint: an average hides flaky questions. An agent that works 2 times in 3 still fails real users. Passing every time measures reliability.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs the experiment went wrong**

- **The rule moved.** The gain or cost limit was set after the numbers came in. Watch for a limit that sits just below the team's result.
- **One try per question.** A team "wins" by a little, then the win vanishes on a rerun. Agents vary from try to try, so a single try can be pure luck.
- **Different questions per design.** One design got easier questions. The scores look far apart, but the comparison isn't fair.
- **Cost per success looks oddly cheap.** Cost was split over all tries instead of only the passed ones. That hides waste.
- **No ablation.** The team wins, but you can't say why. In real use, removing the checker to save money quietly drops quality. An ablation means taking one part out to see what changes.

**Quickest check**

Open the traces for each design. A trace is MLflow's record of one run. Confirm that every question appears the same number of times, 3 to 5, in every design. Then check that the written rule is older than the first run.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three places where this method needs extra care.

**Very few questions.** With only 20 questions, a gain of 3 can come from luck alone, even with 3 tries each. Collect more questions, ideally 100 or more, before trusting a small gain. If you can't, make your written rule demand a bigger gain.

**Things change over time.** Model providers update their models and change their prices, so last month's winner may lose today. Rerun the same experiment on a schedule, with the same rule written down, and compare the new results to the old ones.

**A much bigger system.** With five or six agents, taking out one part at a time (an ablation) means many designs, and each one runs 3 to 5 times. Start by removing the parts you suspect matter most. Set a spending limit for test runs before you begin.

judge.notes: No real problems; the '100 or more' questions figure goes beyond the lesson, but it doesn't contradict it.

learn:term.a:
A **baseline** is the starting point you measure a new idea against.

Think of new running shoes. Before you buy them, you time a mile in your old shoes. Say it takes 9 minutes. That 9 minutes is your baseline. When you try the new shoes, you only care whether they beat 9 minutes. Without that number, a fast run tells you nothing.

In this lesson, the baseline is **one agent**. It's the simple, cheap design you already have. The team is the new idea, so the team has to prove it does better.

Look at the example table. The baseline row is "one agent: 12 of 20 passed every time, $0.04 per success." Every other row is compared to that.

- The team passes 15 of 20. That's 3 more than the baseline. Over 20 questions, that is 1.5 in 10 (0.15). It clears the rule's 0.1 bar, at $0.35, which is under the $0.50 limit.
- The team without its checker passes 12 of 20. That's no better than the baseline. So the checker is what makes the team worth it.

judge.notes: Minor: 'every other row is compared to that' skips the lesson's team vs team-without-checker comparison, but nothing is actually wrong.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Move every helper to a smaller model, then reru…”?
check:0:1.a:
That option gets two things right. Smaller models usually do cost less. And rerunning the eval (your test set that checks the answers are still good) is the right safety check after any change.

What it misses is that you are guessing. Every span is called `"agent"`, so the trace only shows one big total. You can't tell which helper is using most of the 50,000 tokens.

Swapping every helper at once causes three problems:

- **Little gain from some helpers.** Some helpers might use very few tokens, so shrinking them saves almost nothing.
- **Lost quality where it matters.** Some helpers might really need the bigger model, so the team's answers get worse.
- **No clue what broke.** If the eval fails, you don't know which swap caused it. You have to undo everything and start over.

Naming each helper's span first (like `"researcher"` or `"writer"`) splits the total into tokens per helper. Then you can try a smaller model on just the biggest one and test that one change.

**Why the right answer is better:** "Give each helper's span its own name, then see who uses most" turns a blind guess into a measured choice, so you fix the costliest helper first and change only one thing at a time.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Cut the team down to one agent, so it spends fe…”?
check:0:2.a:
It's a fair instinct. Fewer helpers can mean fewer model calls, and fewer calls often means fewer tokens. So the goal is right: spend less.

The problem is that it's a guess. Every span is called `"agent"`, so the trace only shows one big total of 50,000 tokens. You can't see where those tokens go. (A span is a labelled box in the trace around one piece of work.)

Merging everything into one agent might not help much. Say most of the cost comes from reading long documents. A single agent still has to read those same documents, so the biggest cost stays. You'd also be doing a large rebuild without knowing what's expensive. That risks breaking things your eval (your test of whether the team's answers are still good) depends on, possibly for little saving.

A better first step is to measure. Give each helper its own span name, like `"researcher"` or `"writer"`. Then the tokens add up per helper, and you can try a small fix, such as a smaller model, on the costliest one.

"Give each helper's span its own name, then see who uses most" is better because it shows you where the tokens actually go, so you fix the right helper instead of guessing.

check:1:1.q: Why not “A smaller model for every helper at once”?
check:1:1.a:
That option has the right instinct. A smaller model costs less per token, and the researcher would get one too. So the bill would drop.

But look at the numbers. One run uses 50,000 tokens in total. The researcher alone uses 40,000 of them. The writer and checker together use only 10,000. Shrinking their models saves a little money, but it can still make their answers worse.

The bigger problem is what happens if quality drops. Your eval is the set of test questions you rerun to check the team still does its job. If you change three helpers at once and the eval fails, you can't tell which change broke it. You would have to undo everything and start over.

The option also never says to run the eval. Without that check, you don't know if the cheaper team still works.

"A smaller model for the researcher, then rerun the eval" is better because it goes after the biggest cost first, changes only one thing, and tests that one change before you keep it.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Remove the checker, since it costs least”?
check:1:2.a:
That option does one thing right. It uses the per-helper totals from the named spans instead of one big bill. And cutting work can save money.

But it picks the wrong helper. The whole run uses 50,000 tokens. The checker is only 4,000 of them, about 8%. Even removing it completely saves very little.

It also throws away a job. The checker is there to catch mistakes. Without it, bad answers could slip through, and the option never reruns the **eval** (your set of test questions that checks the answers are still good). So you'd save a little money and might lose quality without knowing it.

The lesson's rule is to start with the biggest cost. Here that's the researcher at 40,000 tokens, about 80% of the run. It reads long documents, so it sends lots of input tokens. Making that helper cheaper matters far more than trimming the smallest one.

"A smaller model for the researcher, then rerun the eval" is better because it targets the helper that costs the most and keeps the change only if the eval shows quality still holds.

judge.notes: No real problems. The arithmetic (50,000 total, 8% and 80%) is right. The claim that the checker 'catches mistakes' is inferred from its name, not stated in the lesson, but it doesn't contradict the lesson.

check:2:0.q: Why not “The tokens used by the other helpers”?
check:2:0.a:
That option mixes up two different totals.

**What it gets right:** the other helpers do use tokens, and those tokens count toward the team's bill. Nothing about them is wrong in general.

**What it misses:** the question is about the writer's own total. Tokens per agent means each helper gets its own count, kept in its own named span (a labelled box in the trace). The researcher's tokens belong in the researcher's box, not the writer's. Adding them to the writer would blur the boxes together. Then you can't tell which helper costs the most, and that is the whole point of the lesson.

The real gap is inside the writer's own calls. Each call has two parts: the input tokens you sent and the output tokens that came back. The script only counts the first part. In the lesson's example, the writer sent 900 and got 300 back. The script reports 900, but the true total is 1200.

**Why "The tokens the model sent back" is better:** every model call costs input plus output, so leaving out the output tokens undercounts each helper's own total.

check:2:1.q: Why not “The tokens in your eval questions”?
check:2:1.a:
**Why not "The tokens in your eval questions"?**

It sounds reasonable. Evals do send text to the model, and that text costs tokens. So it's true that evals have a cost.

But it answers a different question. An **eval** is a test you run to check that your agents still give good answers. Its questions are not part of the writer's work in a normal team run. They don't sit inside the writer's named span, so they don't belong in the writer's total.

Also, if an eval question is ever sent to the writer, it goes in as input. Your script already counts input tokens. So adding it wouldn't fill the gap.

The real gap is the other direction. Each model call has two parts: tokens you send in, and tokens that come back. In the lesson's example, the writer's call is `900 in, 300 out`. Your script counts only the `900`. The correct total is `1200`.

**Why "The tokens the model sent back" is right:** tokens per agent is input plus output, and your script is missing the output half.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Name every helper's span” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
The trace adds tokens up **by span name**. A span is a labelled box in the trace that holds one helper's work. If two helpers share a name, the trace treats them as one helper, and their tokens land in one pile.

**Small example.** Say both helpers open their span with `name="agent"`. The lesson's run would then show:

```
agent: 7600
```

That number is true, but you can't act on it. You know the run is costly. You don't know who to fix. You might move the writer to a smaller model. You'd save very little and risk its quality, while the researcher keeps using 6400 tokens.

Name the spans `"researcher"` and `"writer"`, and the same run shows 6400 and 1200. Now the next step is clear. Try a smaller model for the researcher only, and keep it if your eval still passes.

It also matters later. Suppose the bill jumps after a change. With one shared name, you can't see which helper caused it.

With `mlflow.langchain.autolog()`, each LangGraph node's span takes the node's name. So give every node its own name.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Total per helper, then pick the biggest” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

*The problem:* "A multi-agent run has one bill. It's the sum of every helper's model calls. If the trace only shows one total, I can't tell which helper to make cheaper."

*The idea:* "So I give each helper its own named span. That's a labelled box in the trace, like `researcher` or `writer`. Then I add up the input plus output tokens of the calls inside each box. That gives tokens per agent. I start with the biggest one. It's often a helper that reads long documents."

*A trade-off:* "The usual fix is a smaller model for just that helper. Smaller models can give worse answers. So I keep the swap only if my eval still passes. An eval is my automated quality test."

**A likely follow-up**

"A model call's span is often nested a few boxes deep. How do you know which helper it belongs to?"

*Hint at a strong answer:* Climb through the parent spans until you reach the box right under the root. The root is the top box of the trace. That box is the helper. Don't just take the direct parent. A chain span like `RunnableSequence` often sits in between.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs it went wrong:**

- **One big number, no names.** Your trace shows a single total for the whole run. You can't tell which helper to make cheaper.
- **Odd names in your totals.** You see `RunnableSequence` or the root name instead of `researcher` or `writer`. That means you stopped at the wrong box. A "span" is a labelled box in the trace, and model calls often sit a few boxes deep.
- **A helper is missing.** A helper that clearly ran has no total. Its span probably wasn't named.
- **Totals that don't match the bill.** If they come out too low, you may be counting only input tokens and dropping output tokens. If they come out too high, you may be counting the same call twice, for example once at the call and again at a parent box.
- **A cheaper model that "worked" but got worse.** Costs dropped, but you never re-ran your eval, which is your test set. Quality then slips in real use.

**Quickest check:** pick one run. Add up your per-helper totals. They should equal the run's overall token count, and every helper that ran should appear by name.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three places where "add up tokens per helper, fix the biggest" needs extra care.

**1. Helpers use different models.** Tokens are not dollars. Each model has its own price per token, and output tokens usually cost more than input tokens. Some providers also charge less for "cached" input, meaning text they've seen recently. So multiply each call's tokens by that model's prices before you compare helpers.

**2. Helpers call other helpers.** The method climbs to the box right under the root (the top box of the trace). If a "planner" starts a "researcher" inside its own box, all the researcher's tokens get counted as the planner's. Give the inner helper its own named span. Then credit each call to the nearest named helper box above it, not the top one.

**3. One run isn't typical.** A single run might have had an unusually long document. Add up totals across many traces (one trace is the record of one run), and check both the average and the worst runs. A helper that's cheap most of the time but spikes now and then may matter more.

learn:term.a:
A **trace** is a record of everything that happened during one run. A **span** is one box inside that record. It marks when a piece of work started and stopped, and holds what happened in between. A **named span** is simply a box with a label on it, like "researcher" or "writer".

Think of a shared restaurant bill. If you only see the total, you can't tell who ordered the expensive dish. If each person's orders are grouped under their name, you spot it right away.

In the lesson's code, `mlflow.start_span(name="researcher", ...)` creates that labelled box. Every model call the researcher makes lands inside it. If you turn on `mlflow.langchain.autolog()` (automatic recording), each LangGraph node already gets a span named after that node. A node is one step in the graph.

The example shows the payoff. Each call sits inside a labelled box, so you can total them per helper. The researcher's two calls add up to 3400 plus 3000, which is 6400. The writer's one call is 1200. The labels tell you to look at the researcher first.
